paras: The intimidation of a Black newspaper publisher near Paris, Kentucky, was an attack, probably in the first half of 1919, in which white-robed horsemen seized the publisher of a Black-owned paper that had urged local workers to organize. The episode is known only from a minister's report to the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's annual conference, as relayed by the Cleveland Gazette, which said the publisher was terrorized into silence.

The N.A.A.C.P. held its tenth annual conference in Cleveland in late June 1919. Speakers from the South repeatedly protested from the floor that conditions in southern states and cities were intolerable, and the conference platform urged Black workers to organize for their protection.

According to a minister from Paris, Kentucky, a paper "published by an Afro-American" had recently urged workers in "that part [of] Kentucky" to organize "to secure better industrial conditions." In response, he said, white-robed horsemen "dressed after the manner of the [Ku] Klux Klan of the days following the War of the Rebellion" pounced upon the paper's publisher and "terrorized them into silence." The account names neither the publisher, the paper, nor the attackers, gives no date, and describes no injuries.
No report of arrests or of any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Cleveland Gazette carried the minister's statement on 5 July 1919 as a single sentence within its long front-page report on the conference. The paper set the incident beside delegates' remarks that "a new spirit of bitterness" had arisen among Black leaders since the previous year's session, which they traced to new conditions of repression in the South after the war. No other Black-press account of the attack was found.

accounts.label: Minister's report to the N.A.A.C.P. conference
accounts.gist: After a Black-published paper urged workers of the Paris, Ky., area to organize for better industrial conditions, white-robed horsemen dressed like the Reconstruction-era Klan pounced on its publisher and terrorized them into silence.
